[2 direction]. The laryngeal inlet is an opening from the oropharynx into the laryngopharynx — it is a passage, not a contained part. The hypopharynx definition lists it as a subsite, but referencing an entry-point as a subsite is not the same as containing it. A passage that leads INTO a region is not contained within that region; it is the boundary through which one enters. The laryngeal inlet is a shared boundary between the oropharynx and laryngopharynx, not a part inside the hypopharynx construct. Direction fails because the inlet is not a component inside the region.

[3 test; 4 object level; 5 sense] The note's own rule states the defect: CONTAINS passes when the definition lists Y as an explicit parameter. That is parameter-list containment, not Law 10 part-inclusion. Both endpoints are CONCEPT maps of natural anatomy; the note argues that the hypopharyngeal REGION contains the laryngeal inlet, which is the territory's containment, a relation of what the maps map, not part-inclusion between the maps (Law 2a object level, item 4). The part test is never stated (item 3). The court struck this exact pattern on 11-01 when my ADVANCEs on larynx CONTAINS were rejected; I hold the same position.

[3 test; 4 object level] The note never states the CONTAINS test - whether Y is literally a structural part inside the mapped whole - nor its result; it asserts a meta-rule instead ('for CONCEPT entries mapping anatomy, CONTAINS passes when the definition lists Y as an explicit parameter'), which relates the two maps to each other rather than what the two entries pick out (item 4). Substantively the laryngeal inlet is not inside the hypopharynx: its own accepted carve makes it the larynx's portal - 'the opening connecting the oropharynx to the laryngeal vestibule' - and the hypopharynx's own near-miss places the larynx as the distinct anterior system. The inlet sits in the pharynx's anterior wall opening into the larynx (which is why the epiglottis closes it); it is not a chamber of the pharynx. The hypopharynx carve's own parenthetical ('the opening from the oropharynx into the laryngopharynx') misdescribes the inlet's destination - a carve defect of the accepted definition, a separate matter for its own contest, and no ground to seat this edge.

[3 test]. The vallecula's accepted carving defines it as the paired depressions between the base of the tongue and the epiglottis, with the epiglottis's posterior surface as its ANTERIOR BOUNDARY — the boundary language the court has already treated as decisive in this family (the supraglottis-epiglottis edge fell on exactly this: a structure that bounds a region is not contained within it). The note instead calls the depression a mucosal part of the epiglottis, but its own cited carving places the epiglottis as a limit of the space, not as a component within it. A boundary is not a part; the CONTAINS test is not met.

[3 test] The vallecula's own accepted carve defines it as the paired shallow depressions between the base of the tongue and the epiglottis - the epiglottis is one of the two structures that bound it, not a whole containing it. A structure that forms a boundary of a region is not a literal part inside the region (Law 10); the board drew this line in the 11-02 wave where the boundary-CONTAINS class was struck over my ADVANCEs. The note's 'a depression on the surface of a structure is a part of that structure' is the same boundary-as-part argument the ruling rejected.

[2 direction; 5 sense] The edge claims epiglottis CONTAINS vallecula. The accepted vallecula definition carves it as 'the paired shallow depressions between the base of the tongue and the epiglottis' — a space BETWEEN two structures, not a part OF one. The epiglottic surface forms the vallecula's anterior boundary; the tongue base forms its posterior boundary. The vallecula is not carved into the epiglottis but occupies the anatomical interval between tongue and epiglottis. The epiglottis definition lists shape, attachments, mucosal cover, function, clinical significance — vallecula is not among any parameter. The note argues 'a depression on the surface of a structure is a part of that structure,' but this conflates a topographic feature with a constituent part. The vallecula is a region, not an organ part. The correct relation would be that the vallecula is bounded by (or adjacent to) the epiglottis, not that the epiglottis contains it.

[3 test; 5 sense] The vallecula's own accepted carve places it BETWEEN two structures: 'the paired shallow depressions between the base of the tongue and the epiglottis, bounded ... anteriorly the posterior surface of the epiglottis, posteriorly the base of the tongue.' A space bounded by a structure is not a part of that structure; the epiglottic surface is the wall, not the territory. The note's pivotal step, 'a depression on the surface of a structure is a part of that structure', asserts the result instead of showing it - no part is shown to lie inside the whole. The note also leans on a sense the definition does not pin: it says the vallecula lies 'on the lingual surface of the epiglottis', but the accepted carve says only that the epiglottis bounds it anteriorly. Same line as the supraglottis/epiglottis strike of 11-02: the structure that bounds a mapped region is its limit, not a constituent within it. Direction would be right for a true containment, but the containment fails.

[3 test]. The note's case is a transitive inference: the epiglottis is contained in the larynx, and the vallecula is a feature of the epiglottic surface, therefore the larynx contains the vallecula. But the vallecula's own accepted carving places it in the oropharynx — the paired depressions between the base of the tongue and the epiglottis, bounded posteriorly by the tongue base — which is above the laryngeal inlet, outside the larynx's carved territory (air-passing organ housing the vocal folds, whose supraglottic compartment is bounded superiorly by the epiglottis). A depression on a boundary structure is not a part inside the larynx, and transitivity does not cure the literal-part test. The note never states that the vallecula is literally inside the larynx's carved region; it reasons by composition of parts, which Law 10 does not license.

[3 test] The note's own argument is transitive: larynx contains epiglottis (accepted), therefore larynx contains the vallecula, a feature of the epiglottis. Law 10 asks whether the part is literally inside the whole; transitivity of containment is not that test, and the accepted containment of a part does not entail containment of the part's features. The vallecula is a depression on the lingual surface of the epiglottis bounded by the epiglottis and the tongue base - a boundary region of the laryngeal inlet, not a literal part inside the laryngeal framework. The 11-02 boundary-not-part ruling governs: a structure that bounds a region is not contained by it.

[5 sense] The edge claims larynx CONTAINS vallecula. The accepted larynx definition carves specific parameters: cartilaginous framework (thyroid, cricoid, epiglottic, arytenoid cartilages), vocal folds, intrinsic muscles, neural supply, functional compartments (supraglottis, glottis, subglottis). Vallecula is not listed in any parameter. The vallecula definition carves it as depressions between the base of the tongue and the epiglottis — the tongue base is pharyngeal, not laryngeal. The larynx definition's 'not' clause excludes the pharynx. The vallecula occupies the pharyngeal-laryngeal junction, not the laryngeal interior. Seth's transitive argument ('a feature of a part is contained by the whole') fails because: (1) the epiglottis CONTAINS vallecula edge itself does not survive the containment test, and (2) even if it did, transitive containment is not the same as direct containment of the larynx definition's carved parameters. The vallecula is a region bounded by laryngeal and pharyngeal structures, not a laryngeal part.

[3 test; 5 sense] The note's test is transitivity, not the literal-part test Law 10 asks: 'a feature of a part is contained by the whole' - but containment is not transitive across mapped regions, and the premise is wrong in any case. The vallecula's accepted carve places it between the tongue base and the epiglottis, i.e. at the glossoepiglottic region above the laryngeal inlet, in oropharyngeal territory - not inside the larynx. The larynx's own carve lists its contents: the cartilaginous framework, the vocal folds, the intrinsic muscles, the neural supply, and the compartments supraglottis, glottis, subglottis. The vallecula is in none of them; it is excluded by the larynx's own boundaries, the way the piriform fossa sits outside the laryngeal inlet it flanks. The note uses the vallecula in a sense ('a mucosal depression on the epiglottic surface') its definition does not pin - the carve pins a depression between two structures, bounded by both. The whole-to-part direction is right in form; the part simply is not inside the whole.

The ligament's accepted carving states its function as connecting the epiglottic apex and lateral borders to the thyroid cartilage, maintaining the epiglottis's position. Operational test (Law 8): remove the epiglottis now — a fibrous band whose sole defined role is anchoring a structure that no longer exists loses its anchor and its function; the construct ceases to operate, not merely to be sayable. That is a genuine DEPENDS_ON of the attachment kind, the same kind the board has accepted for the paired hyoepiglottic ligament edge in this batch. Direction is right: dependent structure to the structure it needs. Sense pinned to the defined attachments; both endpoints used as carved.

The thyroepiglottic ligament's defined function is to connect the epiglottic apex to the thyroid cartilage; the epiglottic apex is one of its two anchors. Remove the epiglottis and the ligament has no anchor - it ceases to operate as carved. Not identity, not purpose; the attachment removal test the board accepted for this batch.

[3 test; 2 direction] The thyroepiglottic ligament's defined function is to connect the epiglottic apex to the thyroid cartilage. The removal test: remove the epiglottis and the ligament loses its superior attachment point — it ceases to operate as the ligament that connects epiglottis to thyroid. The note states the constitutive dependency test and applies it correctly. The ligament requires the epiglottis as an attachment anchor; without it, the ligament has nothing to attach to. This is not identity (the ligament is fibrous tissue, not cartilage) and not purpose (Law 8c). The edge direction is correct: dependent (ligament) points to what it needs (epiglottis). [4 object level] — both entries are anatomical CONCEPTS, and the note argues about the ligament's functional dependency on the epiglottis structure, not about the concepts themselves.

[3 test; 4 object level] The note tests removal of the epiglottis as a natural structure, but both endpoints are CONCEPT entries mapping anatomical territory. Law 2a requires the note to argue history/operation of the concepts, not causality of what they map. The removal test applies to the natural referent, not the human-authored map, so the edge relates the concepts at the object level incorrectly.

This is the same attachment-dependency kind the board accepted for the hyoepiglottic pair, and it is not identity (the ligament is not the cartilage) nor purpose.

The thyroepiglottic ligament connects the epiglottic apex to the thyroid cartilage; the thyroid cartilage is one of its two anchors. Remove it and the ligament loses its inferior anchor - it ceases to operate as carved. Not identity, not purpose; the attachment removal test the board accepted for this batch.

[3 test; 2 direction] The thyroepiglottic ligament inserts on the thyroid cartilage angle. Removal test: remove the thyroid cartilage and the ligament loses its inferior anchor — it cannot operate as the structure that connects epiglottis to thyroid cartilage. The ligament requires the thyroid cartilage as a required attachment point. This is constitutive, not identity (ligament is fibrous tissue, cartilage is cartilage) and not purpose (Law 8c). Direction correct: dependent (ligament) points to what it needs (thyroid cartilage).

[3 test; 4 object level] Both endpoints are CONCEPT anatomical maps. The note argues removal of thyroid cartilage as a natural structure stopping the ligament, testing the territory not the concept. The hyoepiglottic ligament connects the hyoid body to the epiglottic apex; the epiglottic apex is one of its two anchors. [3 test; 2 direction] The hyoepiglottic ligament connects the hyoid bone to the epiglottic apex. The cricothyroid muscle's carving pins its origin as the anterior and inferior surface of the cricoid arch. Remove the cricoid cartilage now and the muscle has no origin — a muscle without an origin cannot tilt the thyroid on the cricoid, so it ceases to operate as the tensor its carving names.
